*: The preganglionic cell body sits in the lateral horn (intermediolateral column) of the thoracolumbar cord, T1-L2.
Its lightly myelinated axon leaves by the ventral root with the motor axons and reaches a chain ganglion by the white ramus: a short preganglionic fibre.
It synapses (acetylcholine) on the postganglionic cell body in a paravertebral (chain) ganglion‹; gut fibres pass through to prevertebral ganglia›.
One postganglionic route rejoins the spinal nerve, so every cutaneous and motor nerve carries sympathetic axons.
In the skin they reach blood vessels, sweat glands and arrector pili muscles: smooth muscle and glands.
Another long, unmyelinated postganglionic fibre runs from the upper thoracic chain to the heart and releases norepinephrine.
Targets are smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands, here the heart (faster, stronger beat); the adrenal medulla is a modified ganglion.
Preganglionic cell bodies sit in the nuclei of CN III, VII, IX and X (here the dorsal motor nucleus of X) and in the S2-S4 lateral horn.
Their long axons leave in the vagus nerve and run down the neck to the heart and the root of the lung.
They release acetylcholine onto postganglionic cell bodies in small ganglia on or in the organ wall.
A short postganglionic fibre runs in the heart wall and releases acetylcholine.
At the heart the effect is a slower heart rate.
Another short postganglionic fibre reaches the smooth muscle of the bronchial wall.
Targets include the heart, lungs, gut and glands, and (by CN III) the pupil, which constricts.
Taste buds on the posterior tongue and baroreceptors in the carotid sinus are two of the solitary nucleus's inputs (with the aortic arch and gut wall).
Their sensory axons run in CN VII, IX and X; here both run in the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).
The 1st-order cell body sits outside the brainstem, in a ganglion of the cranial nerve.
The axon enters the medulla, runs in the solitary tract and synapses in the solitary nucleus: taste rostrally, visceral input caudally.
The solitary nucleus is the hub for visceral sensation and turns it into autonomic reflexes.
Taste drives salivation through the inferior salivatory nucleus (CN IX).
Its preganglionic parasympathetic neurons leave in CN IX.
CN IX fibres synapse in a ganglion near the gland‹ (otic ganglion, via the lesser petrosal nerve)›; postganglionic fibres reach the parotid.
The parotid gland secretes saliva: taste drives salivation.
Visceral input reaches the nucleus ambiguus (swallowing, speech, airway, heart rate).
The nucleus ambiguus holds the motor neurons of the pharynx and larynx.
Its axons leave in the vagus nerve to the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles.
The pharynx and larynx contract for swallowing and airway protection.
Baroreceptor input reaches the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.
Its preganglionic parasympathetic neurons leave in the vagus nerve (X).
Long vagal fibres synapse in ganglia in the heart wall; short postganglionic fibres reach the heart.
When blood pressure rises, the baroreceptor reflex slows the heart through the vagus.
Taste also reaches the superior salivatory nucleus (CN VII).
Its preganglionic parasympathetic neurons leave in CN VII.
CN VII fibres synapse in a ganglion by the glands‹ (chorda tympani and lingual nerve to the submandibular ganglion)›; postganglionic fibres reach the glands.
The submandibular and sublingual glands secrete saliva.
The caudal solitary nucleus also drives the sympathetic outflow, down the cord to the lateral horn.
Its sympathetic preganglionic neurons leave by the ventral root to the sympathetic chain.
Chain ganglion neurons send postganglionic fibres to the heart and the blood vessels.
When blood pressure falls, the sympathetic outflow speeds the heart and constricts the vessels (baroreceptor reflex).
The motor plan starts in layer V neurons of the cerebral cortex.
Their axons descend through the internal capsule and the cerebral peduncle and synapse on the pontine nuclei of the same side.
The 2nd-order cell bodies sit in the pontine nuclei of the basis pontis.
Their axons cross the midline as the transverse pontine fibres.
They enter the cerebellum through the opposite middle cerebellar peduncle.
They end as mossy fibres in the cortex of the cerebellar hemisphere.
Each cerebral hemisphere informs the opposite cerebellar hemisphere of its motor plan.
Mossy fibres (here from the pontine nuclei; also DSCT and vestibular) and climbing fibres (from the inferior olive) carry the plan and the feedback.
Pontine neurons cross the midline and enter the cerebellum by the middle cerebellar peduncle.
Inferior olive neurons cross the midline and enter by the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Both inputs reach the Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex, the only output of the cortex, which are inhibitory.
Purkinje axons inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei.
The deep cerebellar nuclei are excitatory and are the cerebellum's output.
Their axons leave by the superior cerebellar peduncle.
They cross the midline in the caudal midbrain, at the level of the inferior colliculus.
They end in the contralateral red nucleus and VA/VL thalamus, which projects back to the motor cortex.
The VA/VL thalamus (with the red nucleus) is the next relay: it sends the cerebellum's output on to the motor cortex.
VA/VL axons run up through the internal capsule to the motor cortex on the same side as the thalamus.
This motor cortex drives the body on the cerebellum's own side (its tract crosses again), so a cerebellar lesion affects the same side (double crossing).
The loop starts in the cerebral cortex.
Corticostriate fibres excite the striatum (caudate and putamen).
The striatum is the input nucleus of the basal ganglia.
The striatum inhibits the GPi, which then stops inhibiting the VA/VL thalamus, so the cortex is excited.
The striatum inhibits the GPe, which releases the STN; the STN excites the GPi, which inhibits the thalamus more.
The substantia nigra pars compacta sends dopamine to the striatum: D1 excites the direct pathway, D2 inhibits the indirect.
The GPi is the inhibitory output of the basal ganglia.
The GPi inhibits the VA/VL thalamus, whose excitatory neurons project to the motor cortex.
Too little GPi inhibition of the thalamus gives hyperkinesia (ballismus, Huntington's); too much gives hypokinesia (Parkinson's).
The output neurons of the hippocampus project out through the fornix.
Their axons run in the fornix: crus behind the thalamus, body over it, column down in front of it, to the mammillary body.
The fornix ends in the mammillary bodies, the septal nuclei and the basal forebrain; the circuit consolidates memory, not retrieval.
The output of the amygdala leaves from its central nucleus.
Its axons arch along the caudate in the stria terminalis to the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) and the hypothalamus.
Through the BNST, the hypothalamus and the brainstem autonomic nuclei (dorsal motor nucleus of X), the amygdala drives the body's fear response.
The circuit starts in the septal nuclei of the basal forebrain, near the midline.
Their axons run back along the top of the thalamus in the stria medullaris thalami.
They end in the habenula‹, beside the pineal gland›.
Dopaminergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in the midbrain start the reward pathway.
Their axons run forward in the medial forebrain bundle through the lateral hypothalamus to the nucleus accumbens and on to the prefrontal cortex.
Dopamine released in the nucleus accumbens and the prefrontal cortex signals reward.
